item.title: SoftBank seeks $100 billion for AI-refined projects from Middle Eastern investors — fund would be used to acquire companies and improve their operations using artificial intelligence and robotics
item.description:
Masayoshi Son, founder of SoftBank, is seeking up to $100 billion from Gulf investors to establish a fund that would acquire companies and improve their operations using artificial intelligence and robotics, according to the Financial Times . The initiative comes as SoftBank faces growing concerns over its $65 billion investment in OpenAI and its delayed initial public offering (IPO).

Unlike SoftBank's previous investment vehicles, which primarily financed technology companies, the proposed fund would purchase established businesses and introduce AI and other advanced technologies to improve their operations in a bid to improve their value, which is a relatively novel model to make money on AI. Son has reportedly approached influential investors in the Middle East, including senior figures in the United Arab Emirates, in recent weeks to get the money to acquire companies that have not yet adopted AI and/or robotics, but which could substantially improve their business positions by doing so.

Roze, SoftBank's robotics and physical AI division, would reportedly play a major role in these transformations, though exact details remain unclear. Son also intends to eventually take Roze public at a substantial valuation, though neither the fund's establishment nor its financing is guaranteed. In fact, at this point it is unclear whether the fund will only finance acquisitions, or will also finance development of Roze.

SoftBank has already committed approximately $65 billion to OpenAI, and the company remains the crown jewel of its investment strategy. The Japanese company has financed its investments using internal resources, external capital, and borrowing partly secured by its holdings in Arm. Meanwhile, SoftBank's well-being significantly depends on the valuation of OpenAI, which has yet to become a highly profitable company. Despite risks associated with OpenAI valuation, SoftBank continues to pursue aggressive AI expansion.

Son has previously attracted substantial financing from Middle Eastern sovereign wealth funds. Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund and Abu Dhabi's Mubadala participated in SoftBank's original $100 billion Vision Fund in 2017. Since its establishment, Vision Fund 1 has accumulated approximately $29 billion in investment gains, whereas Vision Fund 2, which holds the OpenAI investment and is primarily financed by SoftBank, has generated $20.5 billion as of June. Abu Dhabi has also expanded its AI investments through MGX and G42.

Last month, SoftBank raised more than $11 billion through the largest junk bond issuance on record, with yields reaching 9.75% (i.e., very expensive borrowing as risks are high). As of June, the company's net asset value stood at ¥72.3 trillion ($456.57 billion), while its loan-to-value ratio was 13%, considerably below its normal operating limit of 25%. However, a substantial portion of SoftBank's assets is tied to technology companies, including Arm and OpenAI, so a decline in their valuations could increase the company's LTV to uncomfortable levels even without further borrowings.

Son's investment history includes Alibaba's massive success and WeWork's 2023 bankruptcy, so it remains to be seen where the current strategy leads SoftBank.

item.title: Super Micro smuggling co-conspirator pleads guilty to sending AI chips to China — broker admits breaking export control rules as company co-founder denies charges
item.description:
Ting-Wei “Willy” Sun, a third-party broker and “fixer” who’s been charged alongside Super Micro co-founder Yih-Shyan “Wally” Liaw and sales manager Ruei-Tsang “Steven” Chang for conspiring to unlawfully divert Nvidia AI chips to China, has pleaded guilty to the allegations against him. According to Bloomberg , Sun’s plea comes as part of an agreement with prosecutors, although the details of any possible cooperation arrangement remain undisclosed. Sun is also expected to be sentenced on Sept. 8, 2027, after entering his plea.

The case against the individuals was revealed earlier this year after it was discovered that they diverted Super Micro servers containing Nvidia chips to China. The three were reported to have sent the servers to a Southeast Asian company, which then proceeded to fake the paperwork and create dummy servers for inspectors. Workers then used hair dryers to remove the serial numbers on the real servers to transfer them to the dummy server shells to complete the illusion, while the real servers made their way to China. Further investigation revealed that the three used a Thailand-based corporation to receive the servers, which were then delivered to Alibaba , even as the Chinese tech giant denied receiving the banned Nvidia hardware.

Super Micro has also denied any knowledge of the operation, even as it has netted $2.5 billion in sales since it started in 2024. Nevertheless, the company’s shareholders have sued it, accusing it of concealing its dependence on illicit sales to China . Liaw, on the other hand, has pleaded not guilty to the charges and was released on a $5 million bond. The Super Micro co-founder is set to go to trial this coming Nov. 2, even as the third co-conspirator, Chang, remains a fugitive.

Taiwanese authorities are also building their own case against the illegal shipment of AI chips to China, with the investigators raiding some Super Micro offices and the homes of six individuals . The company, on the other hand, denied that its premises were raided , insisting that it cooperated with the police and provided access to the workstations and gadgets of the employees that were being investigated. It also said that it has been collaborating with both U.S. and Taiwanese authorities over the smuggling investigation, and that it has even fired several employees after completing its own independent investigation. Soon after this, Taiwan indicted nine more people involved in the illegal smuggling of Nvidia B300 GPUs.

Sun’s guilty plea is the latest development in the U.S.’s clampdown on illegal AI chip exports, which happened soon after another tech CEO was arrested in California for smuggling $300 million in Nvidia AI servers to China. These cases show how serious the White House is about protecting its hardware advantage over Beijing in the AI race, even as AI development is facing its own challenges at home.

item.title: Senate probe accuses Big Tech of misleading public on AI data centers — massive 100 MW sites create only 100 jobs while securing lucrative GPU tax breaks; Senators question the number of permanent jobs, but companies refuse to divulge data
item.description:
The U.S. Senate has been conducting a year-long investigation into AI data centers, and its findings suggest that some developers have been misleading the public about the costs and benefits that these projects bring to their communities. According to Time , data center developers have routinely pointed to the number of construction jobs that projects bring to neighborhoods, but many have allegedly refused to share the number of permanent positions these projects bring to the neighborhood once they’ve reached operational status. A few companies that did give numbers point to a ratio of one permanent position for every megawatt of capacity, meaning a 100-megawatt development, which consumes around the same amount of electricity as 100,000 homes, would only hire 100 people.

  • GTC 2026: Ian Buck press Q&A transcript — VP of Hyperscale and HPC speaks out on shelving CPX and shipping LPU decode this year
  • Demand for data center CPUs has surged, and AI agents are responsible

“Congress must hold Big Tech accountable so these companies pay their fair share,” Senator Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) told the publication. Senator Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) also said, “This report lays bare what we have long known: working Americans and local communities are footing the bill for Big Tech’s massive expansion of data centers, while these companies continue to operate without transparency.”

Aside from the lack of permanent jobs, the authorities also looked at the tax incentives these companies have been getting from local and state governments. The investigation revealed that although property-tax breaks catch critics’ attention during the application process, sales-tax exemptions on computer equipment are reportedly more lucrative, especially as these sites maintain, replace, and upgrade their hardware. The report estimated that 39% of a 1GW data center’s spending is allocated towards expensive GPUs, so if the data centers do not deliver the jobs and economic benefits they’ve promised, then the state is losing out on a lot of revenue.

The investigation also revealed that the surveyed companies — Amazon , Google , Meta, Microsoft , CoreWeave, Digital Realty, and Equinix — don’t want to cover the costs of the additional infrastructure needed to serve their data centers even though they previously promised to “pay their own way.” While the companies said that they were willing to pay for direct costs, they argued that they should not be responsible for the larger investments that could potentially benefit other customers, such as new power plants and transmission lines, even though these were primarily driven by their power demands.

There have already been efforts to legislate the ratepayer protection pledge that data center developers signed earlier this year, but it has failed because senators thought that it was “toothless.” This investigation shows that Congress is not giving up and that it’s conducting an even broader effort to regulate the infrastructure behind AI, especially with regard to its massive power consumption and other issues that residents living around them have been protesting against.

item.title: Top AI labs reportedly planning for catastrophic AI event fallout — Anthropic, OpenAI, and others reportedly building contingency plans and running scenarios of a runaway AI wreaking havoc
item.description:
Anthropic, OpenAI, and other AI labs are reportedly gaming out scenarios where a rogue AI wreaks havoc on critical infrastructure, like financial services, internet and telecommunications, or utilities such as power and water. According to Axios , the leadership of these companies is privately preparing for such an incident, similar to how the Pentagon has been running war games to see the results of different strategies in case of a nuclear exchange between nations.

Planning like this is not unheard of in the corporate world, with enterprises sometimes running business continuity exercises to account for contingencies. However, what’s concerning is that these exercises are in preparation for a major AI incident, something that many industry experts believe would happen within the next six to 12 months. "OpenAI conducts preparedness exercises where teams discuss and work through a range of potential scenarios," a company spokesperson told the publication. "These scenarios are not treated as inevitable but are meant to help us prepare for a variety of circumstances."

Dario Amodei recently released a warning about an AI-driven botnet “swarm” taking over the entire internet in the coming months, especially after incidents of OpenAI’s models escaping their testing environments . We’ve also heard of incidents where a “kill switch” failed to stop a rogue agent , forcing the startup to pause testing. The threat is so great that Anthropic listed “existential risks to humanity” as one of its major risk factors in its IPO prospectus, allocating nearly a third of the document to covering this issue. A former OpenAI safety employee has spoken out about this, saying that the current risks stem from a lack of safety culture — something that the aviation and nuclear industries have already learned through experience.

Despite that, the White House has refused to impose regulations on artificial intelligence, instead preferring to make Nvidia, OpenAI, Anthropic, and other AI labs promise to “self-police” AI development . But even though the current administration is lenient on AI labs and development, Axios says that one of the things that the scenarios focus on is how to educate Congress after a major incident. An event like this would probably result in Congress attempting to slow or shut down AI development, though planners think that such a move would face significant challenges. It will still likely have an impact on the economy, though, especially as big tech has already spent more than $1 trillion in AI infrastructure , with an additional $32 trillion expected to be invested until 2050 .

The heads of Anthropic, OpenAI, and SpaceXAI have all agreed that a slowdown is needed for AI safety, but it’s unclear what steps these companies have taken to put that into effect. While gaming out scenarios like these is par for the course for any major organization, it still doesn’t give us comfort that they’re essentially preparing for “The Day After Tomorrow” of an AI apocalypse.

item.title: Nvidia reportedly halts GeForce RTX 5090 production in favor of AI data center and professional GPUs — impending supply drought expected to drive up prices, RTX 5080 24GB rumored as new gaming flagship
item.description:
Nvidia has reportedly ceased selling its GB202 graphics processors for consumer-grade GeForce RTX 5090-series add-in-boards (AIBs), including 'D' variants for the Chinese market, according to a leaked notice from an unknown factory cited by @hongxing2020 , who tends to have insights into the graphics card market. Another prominent leaker @Zed__Wang confirmed the report and said that from now on the GB202 silicon will be exclusively used on data center and professional graphics cards.

"According to a notification from the factory, Nvidia will no longer manufacture any RTX 5090 models, including the D variants," a message cited by @hongxing2020 reads. "Going forward, the highest-end GeForce graphics card will be the RTX 5080 24GB, while the RTX 5080 16GB version will be discontinued. Please spread the word."

This is, of course, an unverified claim and not an official Nvidia announcement. We asked Nvidia for a comment, though the company has yet to respond. Typically, Nvidia does not comment on rumors.

While the information is strictly unofficial for now, the alleged decision would make considerable economic sense for Nvidia, as the company can sell GB202 processors on data center and professional graphics cards that cost substantially more than the GeForce RTX 5090. In fact, Nvidia's recently introduced RTX Pro 5500 features the same number of CUDA cores — 21,760 — as the GeForce RTX 5090, but comes with 84GB of GDDR7 memory instead of 32GB and targets considerably more lucrative professional visualization (ProViz) and AI applications. Meanwhile, the fully-fledged RTX 6000 Pro with 24,064 CUDA cores and 96 GB of memory can easily sell for $15,000.

By discontinuing GB202-based GeForce products, Nvidia could prevent its relatively inexpensive consumer graphics cards from competing with its own professional accelerators in the lucrative AI sector. Essentially, the company is redirecting its limited semiconductor manufacturing allocation toward higher-margin products without necessarily sacrificing its position in the gaming market, as neither the GeForce RTX 5080 nor RTX 5090 have direct rivals.

Even if Nvidia has indeed discontinued shipments of GB202 processors for consumer graphics cards, GeForce RTX 5090 boards are unlikely to disappear from the market overnight. Nvidia's add-in-board partners, distributors, and retailers likely have inventories of GPUs and finished graphics cards that could sustain availability for some time. However, if Nvidia no longer supplies GB202 processors for GeForce products, the availability of RTX 5090 cards will inevitably decline, which will affect prices of these AIBs.

Meanwhile, Nvidia could be preparing to refresh its GeForce RTX 50-series lineup. The company has long been rumored to be developing GeForce RTX 50 Super graphics cards, including an RTX 5080 Super with 24GB of GDDR7 memory, although their introduction has reportedly been postponed due to memory supply constraints. The rumored GeForce RTX 5080 24GB could therefore represent a revival of these plans, and with no more GeForce RTX 5090 32GB on the market, the new product will have better memory supply.

Nvidia is also developing its next-generation Rubin-based GeForce RTX 60-series GPUs, but recent rumors suggest that these products will not arrive until late 2027, or even 2028. Consequently, if the reports about the discontinuation of the GeForce RTX 5090 are accurate, Nvidia could leave the enthusiast gaming market without a GB202-class flagship for a considerable period, so if you are in the market for the absolute best graphics card , now is the time to get it.

item.title: Crazed modder straps 360mm AIO radiator to laptop, cuts temps to below 40 degrees — performance gains an average of 14% in games and benchmarks
item.description:
YouTube hardcore PC modder TrashBench attached waterblocks, a water pump, and a 360mm radiator to a Metabox laptop with an Nvidia GTX 1060 and Intel Core i7-8750H. This Frankenstein’s monster of a laptop dropped a whole 60℃ on both the CPU and GPU during benchmarks and stress tests and gained an average of 14% after overclocking.

TrashBench, a YouTuber popular for extreme PC modifications involving various watercooling solutions, decided to “fix” laptop cooling by taking a cut-up 360mm AIO from another project and plans to use it on the Metabox P950EP. Metabox is an Australian brand of laptops rebranded from Clevo, an ODM brand from Taiwan that often gets rebranded in various countries. TrashBench intends to use this laptop for his daughter to play Fortnite on.

The modder intended to use the stock AIO pump along with a second waterblock for the CPU, but after testing whether it would be strong enough to push through a second block, TrashBench realized he would need a bigger pump. He also needed to use another waterblock since the new pump was a standalone one, unlike the waterblock and pump combo on an AIO.

Laptop Cooling Is Stupid. I Fixed It. - YouTube
Watch On

The waterblocks were mounted via a 3D-printed holder, then screwed down to the existing holes previously used for the stock heatpipe and blower cooler. More 3D-printed mounts were used to hold the radiator behind the screen of the laptop, but couldn’t be screwed in because the space between the screen and shell was too small. TrashBench reluctantly used Loctite 2-part epoxy to attach the radiator mount onto the laptop.

That’s not all epoxy was used for, as he didn’t forget about the RAM and VRMs. A heatsink was attached to them, with thermal pads bringing the RAM level with the VRMs to use a single heatsink for each cluster. The VRMs had a dab of thermal paste and a spot of epoxy to keep the heatsink in place, making the modification permanent.

After fully assembling everything and attaching the blocks, pump, and radiator with flexible clear tubes using screw hose clamps, TrashBench tested it for leaks. “I think we’re good,” he says, just before a few bubbles passed by.

The laptop uses 19v, while the pump and fans use 12v, so a DC-DC step-down converter was soldered to the original blower fan’s electrical contacts. Unfortunately, the power source powers on as soon as the laptop is turned on, with no way to make them only turn on under load. So the modder used a toggle switch mounted to a 3D-printed plate, screwed onto the bottom shell that had a large gaping hole cut out of it to accommodate the pump and waterblocks.

To allow the laptop to stand, a 3D-printed riser was screwed to the bottom and is the final touch to the build. As ridiculous as it looks, it impresses with its performance, averaging 60℃ below stock, with the CPU and GPU staying well below 40℃ under full load.

Conservative but clear performance gains were seen after benchmarks, but with the amount of temperature overhead, TrashBench decided to see how much more he could get by overclocking, and it was worth it, as Forza Horizon 5 went from 75 FPS to 77, and then to 83 FPS after overclocking.

item.title: Ukrainian drones strike Russia's largest data center, multiple parts of 1.4 million square foot campus knocked offline — second strike in two days targets massive 63 MW Kaluga facility, marks dramatic escalation in war
item.description:
Hot on the heels of a Ukrainian drone strike on a Russian Yandex data center in Sasovo that caused a major outage, a Yandex facility in Kaluga has been struck in a similar fashion. The huge data center was so badly damaged that Russian state media admitted that multiple modules had been removed from service completely.

United24 Media reports that the facility is located in Grabtsevo industrial park and was designed to be the largest Yandex data center in all of Russia. It only entered service in the second half of 2023, lasting three years before this incident.

The Kaluga data center is a sprawling complex that covers around 1.4 million square feet (130,000 square meters). It's so vast that its 63-megawatt power capacity is around 50% higher than some other data centers owned by Yandex. With more than 3,800 server racks, it's perhaps easy to see why it became a target for Ukraine's drone operators. If, of course, the facility was the intended target for the attack — something yet to be confirmed.

As for what all those server racks actually do, it's reported that Yandex's internal services are housed at the facility. It was ultimately built to allow Yandex to expand its cloud offering.

It's as yet unclear how this drone strike is affecting everyday Russians, but the previous Sasovo strike also impacted Yandex Cloud. At the time, users reported problems with Yandex Mail, Disk, Documents, Pay, and Market despite Yandex claiming that key services remained up and running.

Russian state media TASS confirmed the severity of the attack, saying that “Several modules of the Yandex data center in Kaluga have been completely taken out of operation as a result of a UAV attack, [Yandex] reports.”

This incident is just the latest in a run of attacks on digital infrastructure both in Russia and Ukraine. Russian missiles struck a Ukrainian facility earlier this month, taking the world's second-largest torrent tracker offline in the process.

item.title: Gigabyte's latest BIOS update hints at Intel's Raptor Lake Next launch in 2027 — new CPUs may support both DDR4 and DDR5 memory
item.description:
Gigabyte has just confirmed Intel’s plans to introduce new processors compatible with existing LGA 1700 motherboards, with an expected launch in early 2027. According to a press release , Gigabyte is rolling out a new BIOS update to extend support for the upcoming processors across its entire lineup of Intel B760 and H610 motherboards. Owners of supported boards will be able to flash the latest BIOS and upgrade to the new CPUs without replacing their motherboards.

The most interesting bit is that the update covers both DDR4 and DDR5 variants of these motherboard families, allowing existing systems to remain compatible with the upcoming processors. The continued availability of DDR4 compatibility is particularly relevant as rising memory prices have increased the overall cost of building and upgrading a PC. Notably, the announcement does not include certain motherboard series like the Z690, Z790, and B660, which also feature the same LGA 1700 socket.

Gigabyte has not disclosed SKUs, specifications, or pricing of the upcoming processors. However, the early 2027 launch window aligns with previous reports about Intel's rumored Raptor Lake Next lineup. According to previous coverage, Intel is preparing a third refresh of its Raptor Lake architecture based on the LGA 1700 socket, which debuted with the 13th-gen Core desktop processors and was succeeded by the 14th-gen lineup.

Intel’s Robert Hallock, vice president and general manager of Intel’s enthusiast channel business, told Tom’s Hardware Premium in an interview back in August, “LGA 1700 is still a good socket. Lots of people are still interested in DDR4, so we’ll keep offering, and you'll see pricing smooth out over time. It'll come back to normal. That's the plan.” By extending support for the LGA 1700 platform, Intel could potentially give budget-conscious PC builders another option for reusing existing memory and motherboard hardware instead of moving to a completely new platform.

In a separate report, it has been speculated that Raptor Lake Next could adopt Intel's Core 200 branding, spanning across Core 3, Core 5, and Core 7 models. According to leaked specifications shared by tipster Jaykihn, the range could include a 20-core Core 7 model with 8 Performance cores and 12 Efficient cores rated at 65W; a 16-core Core 5 with 8 P-cores and 8 E-cores rated at 125W; a 10-core Core 5 with 6 P-cores and 4 E-cores rated at 65W and equipped with 24MB of L3 cache; and an entry-level, four-core Core 3 featuring only P-cores, also rated at 65W.

item.title: Independent tests rank Mistral’s new trillion-parameter Large 4 the best AI model outside the U.S. and China — but Chinese open-weights still overcome Europe's best efforts
item.description:
Mistral launched its trillion-parameter Large 4 (ML4) model this week, saying it “pushes the frontier of open-weight performance.” Artificial Analysis (AA), an independent AI benchmarking firm, ranked Mistral's Large 4 as the best model available from outside the U.S. and China in its index. The mixture-of-experts model, trained on Nvidia’s Grace Blackwell GPUs, scored its personal best in AA’s CyberGym-E2E-AA end-to-end cybersecurity measure, although several Chinese open models beat it overall.

See more

ML4 scored 38 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v4.3.2, which AA says makes it the “most intelligent model from outside the US and China." At least five Chinese open models scored higher on the index: DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (max) at 39, GLM-5.3-Flash at 42, Kimi K3 (max) at 44, GLM-5.3 (max) at 45, and MiMo-V2.6-Pro at 46. While MiMo-V2.6-Pro is comparable in total size to ML4, GLM-5.3-Flash is about one-third the size at 320B parameters total and 18B versus ML4’s 49B–52B active. Unlike the rest, ML4 isn’t open yet: Mistral says its weights are due “by the end of the month.”

Mistral bets on this, saying ML4 is “state-of-the-art among open models” on enterprise workloads such as “cybersecurity, finance and law,” and that in visual grounding, where its 1.6B-parameter vision encoder comes in, it can go as far as “surpassing even frontier closed models.” On AA’s Cyber Index, Mistral says, ML4 ranks “among the top five models globally,” and it solves 93% of Cybench, a set of 40 challenges drawn from security competitions.

CEO Arthur Mensch went further in Abu Dhabi, saying the model is “above the Chinese models on certain aspects, including cyber,” Reuters reported. Mistral’s other figures include DeepSWE v1.1 at 61.7%, Coding Agent Index at 49.8%, AutomationBench at 59.9%, and Dense 200 at 42%; AA’s own chart puts ML4 at 27% on Terminal-Bench 4.0.

ML4 does, in fact, beat OpenAI’s closed GPT-6 Luna (max) on CyberGym-E2E-AA, but Luna matches ML4’s 38 on AA’s index at about one-sixteenth of the cost per task ($0.07). Mistral says frontier models such as Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra “score near zero on the same test because they refuse to perform the task,” and AA’s chart marks both as declining some tasks on safety grounds.

Outside of that test, Mistral says ML4 also beats DeepSeek V4 Pro 0813 and Qwen3.8 Max on the Coding Agent Index; per AA, it is cheaper than the latter. Overall, AA’s index-vs.-cost chart puts ML4 below the Pareto line and just outside the “Most attractive quadrant.”

The cost comes from needing 200 million output tokens to run AA’s index, against a median of 81 million. As for speed, ML4 generated 116.1 tokens per second, with 1.46 seconds to the first token. This puts ML4 at about 33% faster than its tier median and 2.6x faster to the first token. AA’s speed is measured on Mistral’s own API, which Mistral says runs on the same hardware the model used for training.

ML4 was “trained from scratch on 3,800 NVIDIA Grace Blackwell GPUs in Mistral’s own datacenters in Europe,” the company said. This is up from 3,000 Nvidia H200s used to train Large 3, released last year, which was smaller at 675B total parameters with 41B active. The training occurred over “roughly two months,” as reported by VentureBeat .

Mistral raised a €3 billion Series D in what the company calls “the largest equity round ever raised by a European technology company” in its post. Mistral Compute has planned for 18,000 Grace Blackwell chips , as announced with Nvidia last year. Mistral says it is “significantly scaling up our compute capacity in our own European datacenters,” and that ML4 will become the base for “a new generation of specialized and optimized Mistral models.” The model’s open weights, once released, will be able to run on a private cloud or on-premises.

The weights, architecture details, and additional benchmarks are expected before the end of October. Artificial Analysis lists the preview as proprietary until the weights arrive. Once it does, the model may be re-scored, and Mistral’s claims will be held to task. For the first two weeks following release, ML4 can be used via API at a discounted rate.

item.title: AMD tried to crush the 'megahertz myth' 25 years ago today, debuting its Performance Rating system — Athlon XP chips introduced the scheme, which endured until Intel lost its clock advantage, focus shifted to multi-core
item.description:
A quarter century ago today, AMD launched its AMD Athlon XP processor family . These were highly performant processors based on the firm’s latest Palomino core, but ran at lower raw clock speeds than Intel rivals. Facing a marketing imbalance between perceived and actual performance, AMD mounted a serious campaign to explode the 'megahertz myth' with this generation of CPUs. Thus, it introduced new Athlon XP processors with a Performance Rating (PR) designation, alongside a slogan insisting “Performance matters more than MHz.”

Intel, with its Pentium 4 processors, was clearly winning the MHz race at the time, while a CPU’s clock speed had long been established by marketers as a key performance metric. Unfortunately for AMD, its CPUs of the era didn’t hit such high clocks, even though the application and gaming performance was just as good (if not better) than Intel's.

Thomas Pabst's view

Our tests from October 2001 noted that AMD wisely undersold its chips, using the newly devised PR naming system. Anything less and it would have faced strong opposition and derision. Our tests clearly showed that a new “AthlonXP 1800+ is able to beat Intel's flagship Pentium 4 2 GHz in the majority of benchmarks ,” wrote the original Tom, Thomas Pabst, in a 13-page feature about AMD’s newest CPUs. Moreover, it was observed that “AthlonXP at 1533 MHz is able to reach or even beat Pentium 4 running at an almost 33% higher clock speed.” Pabst concluded that AMD’s clocks/performance situation forced this concerted stand against the MHz myth.

As we broke the news about AMD’s Performance Rating system, some almost straight-away alluded to it being a ‘Pentium Rating’ system, but it was very early days. We didn’t know whether it would become a long-term success. It was known that AMD planned to establish an independent institution to create a new performance measure that is fairer and more realistic than the current MHz system in the following year. But, of course, Intel wouldn’t be interested in validating that. Pabst concluded that “I might not like it too much,” but admitted AMD had little alternative marketing-wise in the Pentium vs. Athlon era at the beginning of the millennium.

Please stop, it hertz

The AMD PR system would be abandoned roughly five years after it was initiated. Subsequent AMD (and Intel) architectures stopped the rating from making practical sense as the market evolved. For example, Intel’s big MHz advantage was lost in the transition from Pentium 4 Netburst to Pentium M /Core chips. Then, the Athlon 64 was so well received by reviewers and enthusiasts that AMD probably felt it might be wise to finish with its inferiority complex PR system that tied it to its obvious rival. Lastly, by the end of the AMD PR era, the marketing fight was clearly going multi-core . CPU marketing and naming completely sidelined any hint at CPU clock speeds later in the noughties.

item.title: GlobalFoundries to produce silicon interposers for TSMC's CoWoS in the US — Five-year agreement valued at $2 billion
item.description:
GlobalFoundries and TSMC have entered into a five-year manufacturing agreement valued at $2 billion under which GlobalFoundries will produce silicon interposers for TSMC's CoWoS advanced packaging technology. The arrangement will establish a U.S.-based manufacturing source for these components, which will enable TSMC's clients to brand their products as completely made and packaged in America. Volume production is scheduled to ramp up in the first half of 2028.

"By providing manufacturing service using GF's trusted U.S. manufacturing footprint, we are creating a secure, scalable source of essential advanced-packaging elements that will help customers accelerate innovation and strengthen the semiconductor supply chain," said Ed Kaste, senior vice president of CMOS Business at GlobalFoundries.

GF and TSMC team up

Under the agreement, GlobalFoundries will expand manufacturing capacity at its fabrication facility in Malta, NY, to produce silicon interposers used in TSMC's CoWoS-S packaging ecosystem. Such interposers are custom pieces of silicon that provide high-density connections between logic chiplets and high-bandwidth memory (HBM) stacks and enable the creation of complex multi-die processors for artificial intelligence (AI) and high-performance computing (HPC) applications. The companies have not disclosed the production capacity to be installed, but the agreement provides a framework for additional expansion depending on demand.

Silicon interposers used for TSMC's CoWoS-S packaging technology are customized for particular processor designs, as their configurations depend on the number, dimensions, and placement of logic chiplets and HBM stacks, as well as the interconnections between them.

In addition, interposers must meet the power-delivery requirements of specific processors, including power distribution networks and embedded deep trench capacitors (DTC), and their designs must account for signal integrity, power integrity, and thermal characteristics. Furthermore, large interposers may exceed the maximum lithographic reticle size and therefore require stitching, so it remains to be seen how well GlobalFoundries will stitch such interposers for extra-large system-in-packages (SiPs).

While certain manufacturing processes and structural elements can be standardized, the resulting interposers are generally application-specific. GlobalFoundries will not be a TSMC supplier, but a subcontractor that will manufacture multiple customer-specific interposer designs rather than standardized components that require close cooperation with TSMC. Specifically, GlobalFoundries will need to ensure compatibility between its design rules, manufacturing processes, and qualification procedures so that interposers produced by GF can be used in TSMC's CoWoS packaging flows. It remains to be seen how the companies will handle ownership and protection of intellectual property, as interposer layouts may incorporate technologies and production methods specific to TSMC and its customers.

By transferring some interposer production to GlobalFoundries, TSMC could free up some of its own manufacturing resources and increase availability of components required for advanced packaging.

Manufacturing silicon interposers is only one part of the CoWoS-S production process. The technology also requires attaching logic chiplets and HBM stacks to interposers using high-precision bonding equipment, assembling the resulting structures onto organic substrates, and then performing electrical testing. These operations require dedicated manufacturing capacity, which the agreement between the two companies does not address.

Becoming a part of TSMC's CoWoS ecosystem

Following its exit from development of leading-edge process technologies in 2018 and consequent inability to produce leading-edge AI and HPC accelerators, GlobalFoundries is now becoming a part of TSMC's advanced packaging supply chain in the U.S. that will supply custom components for AI and HPC processors.

For GlobalFoundries, the agreement represents an opportunity to participate in the manufacturing of advanced AI processors without producing their leading-edge logic dies. Although the company abandoned the development of leading-edge process technologies eight years ago, its manufacturing capabilities remain suitable for producing certain components used in sophisticated multi-chip packages, including CoWoS-S interposers. It remains to be seen though whether it can also participate in TSMC's CoWoS-L supply chain.

The agreement with GlobalFoundries is particularly important considering TSMC's plans to establish advanced packaging operations in Arizona. The company intends to introduce CoWoS and 3D-IC packaging capabilities in the state before 2029 and has signed a 10-year agreement with Amkor Technology, which is building an advanced packaging facility in Peoria, Arizona, that is scheduled to begin production in early 2028.

As GlobalFoundries ramps up interposer production in New York in the first half of 2028, TSMC could potentially establish a largely domestic CoWoS supply chain that comprises logic dies manufactured in Arizona, silicon interposers produced in New York, and advanced packaging and testing performed by TSMC and/or Amkor in Arizona. For a while, HBM stacks would still have to be sourced from memory manufacturers in Asia, though both Micron and SK hynix intend to bring HBM assembly facilities to the U.S. already this decade, so it is safe to say that the U.S. will have a vertically integrated supply chain for production of advanced AI processors by 2029 – 2030.

There is a catch, though, as GloFo and TSMC have not disclosed how CoWoS assembly operations will be divided between TSMC and Amkor, or whether GlobalFoundries' interposers will be used in Arizona at all. Yet, GF's wording about a trusted U.S. manufacturing footprint strongly implies that its interposers will be primarily aimed at SiPs fabricated entirely in the U.S. Meanwhile, expanding interposer production alone will not increase the number of finished AI processors unless sufficient chip-on-wafer assembly and testing capacity is available.

Some things remain unclear

The initial agreement covers five years and establishes a mechanism for further capacity additions. However, the companies have not disclosed the planned manufacturing volumes, capital expenditures associated with the expansion, or the breakdown of the $2 billion agreement. Furthermore, we yet have to find out how GF's manufacturing capabilities are aligned with CoWoS-S' advancements.

item.title: U.S. suspends green card path for H-1B workers at Microsoft and Adobe — labor certification program blocked due to alleged fraud
item.description:
During a Thursday announcement, Vice President JD Vance said that well-known tech companies Microsoft and Adobe are now blocked out of the PERM program — one of the possible paths for the firms' H-1B workers to eventually evolve to green card status. The move was triggered by alleged fraud and abuse. IT outsourcing firms Cognizant, Infosys, Tata Consultancy, Wipro, HCL, and Capgemini also got slapped with suspensions.

The companies involved have not yet commented.

The administration is not going to process any new or pending Permanent Labor Certification applications for the companies. In a press conference, Vance had harsh words about Microsoft in particular, stating that "There has been no company in the United States, unfortunately, that has abused this system more." He added that "if you do the math, for every worker that Microsoft laid off, they replaced that worker with one and a half foreign indentured servants."

According to Vance, Microsoft fired 6,000 workers while simultaneously benefiting from 6,300 H-1B approvals and nearly 3,000 green cards. The VP said the company filed 3,682 PERM applications, 1,000 of which were for positions that seemingly overlapped with those of laid-off workers. Both Microsoft and Adobe's PERM privileges were cut "due to multiple active federal investigations," as stated by Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling.

A move so swift and harsh is unusual, but it comes against a backdrop of the U.S. government putting a tighter grip on the H-1B program. Last July, the Labor Department launched a nationwide investigation into fraud and human trafficking in H-1B and PERM programs. The inquest focuses on fraudulent applications, wage kickbacks, coercion, below-wage labor, recruitment abuse, and benching — when a company keeps the H-1B employee on the books but doesn't assign them work or pay them.

In September, President Trump signed an executive order aiming to curb abuse of the H-1B program. Cognizant also had its green card filings suspended during that month. The H-1B lottery rules had already changed to reportedly favor highly skilled, highly paid workers.

According to the National Foundation for American Policy and reported estimates , Amazon had the most approved H-1Bs in fiscal year 2025 with 4,644 visas, followed by Meta at 1,555, Microsoft with 1,394, and Google at 1,050.

item.title: Finland orders Google to stop work on two AI data centers over alleged deforestation — company admits it has 'fallen short of our own high standards in this instance'
item.description:
Google subsidiary Tuike Finland Oy has just received a notice from the Finnish Licensing and Supervision Agency, or LVV, ordering it to stop construction on two data centers. According to CNBC , the sites in Muhos and Kajaani cannot proceed until environmental impact assessments have been completed, which have been under investigation for allegedly clearing over 740 acres of Finnish forest for the project.

“We understand the concerns and have fallen short of our own high standards in this instance,” a Google spokesperson told the publication. “We acted in good faith under the Forestry Act and ran nature surveys and put in place measures to protect high-value areas. As we continue our long-term work in the region, we are advancing our landscaping and biodiversity plans, which include tree planting across 130 hectares at Muhos.”

Finland is sometimes called the “Texas of Europe” when it comes to data centers because of its readily available supply of land and electricity, which have been some of the major bottlenecks that data center developers have been facing. Even though the epicenters of the AI data center infrastructure build-up are centered around the U.S. and China, Europe is trying to catch up with its massive $30 billion investment and a target of 100,000 AI GPUs for each site . SoftBank also plans to invest $87 billion specifically in France because of its nuclear-powered electricity grid.

However, other European nations are struggling with the demand for this power-hungry infrastructure. Denmark has paused new data center connection requests as demand hit 60GW — more than eight times the country’s peak power consumption of around 7GW — while Amazon ’s data center projects on the continent are facing delays of up to seven years as they wait for new connections.

These stop-work orders aren’t related to electricity supply, though. Instead, the concerns stem from the alleged cutting of trees without the go-signal from the government. The LVV ordered the subsidiary to stop removing trees and topsoil, as well as cease activities such as excavation, quarrying, crushing, soil mass transfers, ditching, and road and storage construction. “In our opinion, the measures in question will change the environment and cause impacts, the identification and assessment of which are among the key objectives of the EIA procedure,” LVV environmental department head Tommi Muilu said in a statement. Still, the subsidiary can proceed with planning, measurement, soil surveys, and other activities that would only have minimal impacts.

U.S. data centers have increasingly faced resistance from residents and communities around them, with 45 projects worth $68 billion blocked in the second quarter of 2026. We haven’t seen the same level of high-profile opposition in Europe, but this is likely because of the stricter permitting and review processes in the region, where concerns are usually raised and addressed even before construction begins.

item.title: Software could be the easiest fix for hyperscalers' AI power squeeze, researchers say — data center demand is expected to rival Japan's electricity usage by 2030
item.description:
Data center energy demand is shooting constantly upwards. By 2030, some 945TWh of electricity is expected to be used to meet AI’s demand; the International Energy Agency believes — that's as much electricity as Japan uses today. The energy crunch is inescapable, and the industry’s answer has largely been to focus on the physical: build more efficient GPUs and secure more power supply from an already tight grid. But is that myopic focus on hardware actually worth it? Instead, could most of the work running on those machines be cut back to save power?

Average power usage effectiveness (PUE) has barely changed for six successive years, according to the Uptime Institute’s 2025 survey . PUE can show whether cooling and power systems are wasteful, but doesn’t account for whether the software running on the servers is doing useful work. And given servers account for around 60% of electricity demand in a modern data center, while cooling ranges from about 7% in an efficient hyperscale site to more than 30% in a less-efficient enterprise facility, focusing on eking out more efficiency from the software side of the equation seems sensible.

“The answer to what seems to be the core question – ‘Can software or algorithms meaningfully help with power and energy?’ – is yes, 100%,” said Jae-Won Chung, a PhD candidate in computer science and engineering at the University of Michigan and researcher with the ML.Energy initiative , in an interview with Tom’s Hardware Premium .

Chung suggests computing systems should be seen as a stack with hardware at the bottom, backed up by systems software, algorithms and applications. The hardware end of that equation is the hardest bit to tackle: chips are slow and costly to replace. But the other three layers are easier to change, and any gains in efficiency made there can compound.

ML.Energy’s tests of the Alibaba Qwen 3 235B A22B Thinking model suggest that running inference in FP8 – a slightly lower-precision format – consumed a third less energy than bfloat16 versions on problem-solving tasks. Chung’s ow n Perseus training optimiser identifies parts of a large-model training job that have less work to do, then slows them so they finish alongside busier parts. The system cut training energy by up to 30% without reducing throughput or changing the hardware.

This isn’t a tweak around the edges being made by tinkerers: some of the biggest GPU firms are doing something similar. Nvidia’s Blackwell power profiles fine-tune everything from GPU compute and memory frequencies, power limits, NVLink states and cache settings to fit the workload. Nvidia believes that can save up to 15% of energy while retaining 97% or more of overall performance, allowing power-constrained facilities to run more GPUs, raising throughput by as much as 13%.

‘The loudest rack in the room’

Chetan Visrolia, business development manager for data center infrastructure at SHI, said in an interview with Tom’s Hardware Premium that the most obvious waste he encounters is often legacy equipment supporting old code. “It is always the lowest-hanging fruit for quick savings,” he said. “It can easily be found in any data center, as it is the loudest rack on the floor.”

Cloud instances can also be made a smarter size, and AI prompts that are repeatedly used can be stored in cache rather than recomputed on the fly. There are also efficiencies to be made by getting small models to handle routine requests while holding back the larger ones for harder tasks. At the same time, better batching and compilers can raise accelerator utilisation, and crunching down prompts while throwing limits on outputs can also tamp down the number of tokens processed.

Software can also change when and where electricity is drawn. Sophie Hall, a doctoral student at ETH Zurich’s Automatic Control Laboratory who has studied workload shifting across Google ’s global data-center fleet, argues in an interview with Tom’s Hardware Premium that electricity consumption isn’t necessarily the main problem.

“It’s more like: when do they use it, where do they use it, and how is it interacting with the grid?” she said. If batch jobs aren’t time-sensitive, they could be delayed until local demand falls or routed to a region with spare capacity and lower-carbon electricity. Hall’s research uses day-ahead planning and real-time scheduling to respond to grid signals while preserving performance guarantees.

Taking that kind of action was less necessary when hyperscalers built way more capacity than they actually needed and the grid wasn’t a bottleneck, Hall said. But the massive demand for AI has changed the equation.

There are limits, though: individual countries’ data sovereignty rules can prevent a workload from crossing borders, while moving large datasets across networks is something that inference providers may be wary of in case things go wrong. “The data needs to literally, physically, geographically move to a different location,” Hall said. “That’s not that easy.”

The scale of the data center demand powered by AI means that software isn’t a silver bullet or a substitute for better chips and new electricity infrastructure. But it can act as a control layer that squeezes out every last drop from those increasingly expensive assets, while also helping shift demand to places where there is more capacity.

Jevons ’ paradox is also at play, and needs to be considered when thinking about making systems run better. Efficiency doesn’t reduce a facility’s electricity use if each watt saved gets used up generating even more tokens. “Power is the core bottleneck in AI data centers,” said Chung. “We really want to make the best use of every watt we consume.”

item.title: Ukrainian drones hit Russia's Yandex data centers housing two top supercomputers — major outage follows retaliatory strike
item.description:
Ukrainian drones hit a major Yandex data center in Sasovo, Russia, causing a massive fire and forcing the company to shut down the facility, according to Reuters and Meduza . Many services using Yandex Cloud are down following the attack. The site reportedly houses two of Yandex's three supercomputers used for artificial intelligence development, though it remains unclear whether the systems sustained any damage, as for now their fate is unclear. Russian missiles struck Ukrainian digital infrastructure earlier this month .

The Sasovo facility, one of Yandex's five major data centers, accommodates tens of thousands of servers, including two Nvidia A100-based supercomputers named Chervonenkis and Lyapunov. Chervonenkis, the company's most powerful system, was once ranked as the world's 19 th most powerful supercomputer in the Top 500 list in 2021, but by today's standards its 21.53 FP64 PFLOPS is enough only for the 101 st place in the list. Due to Western sanctions, Yandex can no longer upgrade the system. Both machines have been used to train AI models, including YandexGPT, Russia's leading large language model. Yandex's third supercomputer, Galushkin, is located in Vladimir.

So far, the company has not disclosed whether its supercomputers were affected by the strike, though judging by the massive fire caused by the drone incident, the systems' chances of survival are low. The potential damage to Nvidia-powered computing infrastructure could be extremely painful for Russia's AI industry, which is already constrained by restrictions on exports of advanced AI accelerators and servers to Russia. If the machines are indeed destroyed or damaged, many of its elements may be lost forever, and Yandex will be forced to use Chinese infrastructure for future model training.

The attack also disrupted Yandex Cloud infrastructure, so the company is recommending customers use alternative zones. Although Yandex claims that its key consumer services remained operational, users reported problems with Yandex Mail, Disk, Documents, Pay, and Market. Other affected services reportedly included Cian, Litmarket, Russian Railways, Spartak Moscow, cryptocurrency exchange Rapira, Astral, and the 1C business solutions. Corporate systems operated by T-Bank, Ozon, and Wildberries also experienced disruptions, according to Meduza . A Moscow-region bus operator suspended online ticket sales, while Detector404 registered 58,268 complaints over 24 hours. Many Russian media outlets, including state propaganda RIA Novosti, Vesti, and Interfax, were also down following the attack on 'infrastructure partner,' reports RBC .

It is noteworthy that the Yandex data center occupies former premises of the Sasta machine-tool factory, where Yandex established operations in 2014. Sasta manufactures industrial equipment supplied to various Russian manufacturers, including defense-related enterprises, and is therefore under Western sanctions. Regional authorities reported a fire at an industrial facility following the attack, but it remains unknown whether the intended target was the factory or Yandex's computing infrastructure. Still, no matter the target, Ukraine's sanctions against Russia's economy and military complex seem to be generally more efficient than those imposed by the West.

The incident follows Russian strikes against Ukrainian telecommunications and computing facilities. Since September 23, attacks have damaged or destroyed data centers that belong to at least eight Ukrainian companies, including Virtual Systems, MiroHost, CosmoNova, DataGroup, and CityHost. Among other websites, popular torrent trackers 1337x and NordicQuality temporarily went offline after servers that hosted them were damaged.

Ukraine is consequently moving some digital infrastructure underground, while Russian businesses are discussing deployments in countries considered friendly by Moscow, which is probably limited to just a few states, including China.

"We are going to talk about our broader partnership," said Lisa Su when asked by reporters about what she planned to discuss with Samsung's executives. "We have many partners at Samsung."

Before visiting Samsung headquarters, Lisa Su and Jack Huynh, senior vice president and general manager of AMD's Computing and Graphics Group, attended the AMD Gamer Day event where Su and Huynh answered some questions from South Korean journalists and called local memory makers 'important strategic partners,' something that reflects the significance of data center-grade DDR5 and HBM memory for the company's AI and data center businesses.

"Samsung Electronics and SK hynix are key supply-chain partners for AMD," Su said, Chosun reports. "AI demand is extremely high, so we are planning our long-term supply chain with our partners. […] It is important to plan three to five years ahead with our partners."

The non-binding MOU that AMD and Samsung signed this March covered four areas and remained in effect for a period of three years:

  • Supply of next-generation memory products, including HBM4 and advanced DDR5;
  • Co-development and optimization of memory solutions for Al and high-performance computing systems;
  • Exploration of foundry manufacturing opportunities for the future AMD platforms;
  • Co-optimization of advanced packaging and related semiconductor technologies.

While Samsung has become a principal supplier of HBM4 for AMD's Instinct MI400-series accelerators, expansion of collaboration beyond memory supply is considerably more complicated, as it involves considerable efforts to design chips for Samsung Foundry's process technologies as well as risks associated with a product ramp at a new contract chipmaker. Truth to be told, AMD already uses Samsung Foundry and UMC to make its "ICs in the form of programmable logic devices" however, moving production of more advanced products to Samsung is risky. Meanwhile, Samsung badly needs big customers like AMD, and the latter's dependence on HBM supply certainly gives the former leverage.

"If we transition the production of some of our products to new manufacturers, we may experience delayed product introductions, lower yields or poorer performance of our products," AMD wrote in its most recent Annual Report .

AMD has already started shipments of its Instinct MI455 accelerators with 432GB of HBM4 memory onboard as well as rack-scale Helios AI systems to interested parties.

"We have started shipping our next-generation MI455 and Helios systems," Su told journalists, according to Chosun . "These are all systems that use HBM4."

So, it looks like the company is negotiating for more memory supply. The question is, will it take a risk and adopt Samsung Foundry for something more serious than niche programmable chips in a bid to get more high-bandwidth memory and sell more expensive AI accelerators? Only time will tell.

item.title: AMD's EPYC Verano AI host CPU will reportedly use a special SB1 socket — Zen 6 chip pairs 72 cores with a 24-channel LPDDR5X memory subsystem
item.description:
AMD's upcoming EPYC 9006-series 'Verano' CPUs that are specifically designed for AI servers will use an all-new SB1 socket and will require different cooling systems than other processors in the lineup, according to a listing at Dynatron , a leading maker of server coolers, discovered by InstLatX64 . The new SB1 socket will be smaller than SP7 and SP8 sockets for other Zen 6-based EPYC CPUs and will therefore have different power and cooling needs.

AMD's Verano is quite different from conventional EPYC processors. The CPU will feature up to 72 Zen 6 cores operating at up to 5 GHz and a massive 24-channel LPDDR5X memory subsystem that uses replaceable SOCAMM2 modules. AMD positions Verano as a host processor for AI servers, where CPUs primarily orchestrate workloads running on AI accelerators rather than provide maximum general-purpose performance themselves. Such specialization could explain why AMD developed SB1 instead of using SP7, which accommodates up to 256-core EPYC 'Venice' processors, or SP8, designed for models with up to 128 cores. Meanwhile, AMD has not disclosed SB1's specifications, dimensions, or capabilities just yet.

In fact, given Verano's highly specialized role as a host processor for AI accelerators, AMD may not need to offer a broad range of Verano SKUs typical of its general-purpose EPYC families. If Verano is deployed in systems with a predetermined number of Instinct accelerators, AMD could offer just one or a small number of CPU configurations to ensure a consistent ratio of CPU cores, memory bandwidth, and host-to-accelerator connectivity per GPU and simplify power, cooling, and system qualification, something that Nvidia does with its Grace and Vera processors.

If AMD decided to take a page from Nvidia's book, this explains why it intends to use a dedicated SB1 socket instead of using existing ones. Rather than supporting a broad range of CPU configurations compatible with SP7 and SP8 sockets and systems, SB1 could be optimized for one or a few CPU SKUs, their 24-channel LPDDR5X memory subsystem, and a particular system topology. Note that AMD has not announced how many Verano SKUs it plans to offer, so consider our thoughts speculation for now.

Dynatron's preliminary SB1-4U-Active cooler provides the first indication of what cooling Verano will require. The 4U unit measures 128.05 × 106.6 × 130.7 mm and uses an aluminum fin stack combined with a vapor chamber and heat pipes. The unit is equipped with a double-ball-bearing fan that operates at up to 6,000 RPM and delivers up to 91.7 CFM of airflow, which makes it a quite powerful device.

It is noteworthy that these specifications are virtually identical to those of Dynatron's J26 4U cooler for AMD's much larger SP7 CPUs, to the degree that even the dimensions are similar. This may either indicate that Dynatron reused the J26 design for SB1, or simply copied and pasted J26's specifications onto the SB1-4U-Active cooler's product page to use them as placeholders until the actual cooler is finalized.

For now, Dynatron does not specify the cooler's maximum supported processor power, so its listing cannot currently be used to determine Verano's TDP with confidence. Nevertheless, a large vapor-chamber-based 4U active cooler suggests that Verano will be a server processor with a rather high power consumption despite having considerably fewer cores than the higher-end EPYC 'Venice' CPUs for general-purpose workloads.

AMD plans to launch Verano in the second half of 2027.

item.title: Former Groq engineers sue board over $20 billion Nvidia deal, saying it handed Nvidia the LPU and the team that built it — plaintiffs allege the board kept billions from other shareholders
item.description:
Two former Groq engineers are suing Groq’s former board and former CEO Jonathan Ross, alleging the board handed over employees and company technology to Nvidia in a $20 billion deal. The proposed class action, filed in Delaware’s Court of Chancery by Benjamin Serebrin and Joshua Rubin and unsealed Monday, alleges the deal, with a $17 billion license fee for all backers and a separate $3 billion Nvidia stock pool for engineers who transferred, kept billions from other shareholders. Meanwhile, Groq is planning to deploy its own technology, now Nvidia’s Groq 3 LPX, the Financial Times reports.

Nvidia’s annual report (10-K) books $14.4 billion of the license as goodwill “primarily attributable to the workforce and future development of the licensed technology” plus $2.5 billion for the technology itself. The plaintiffs concede that “no Delaware decision has directly answered the question this case raises,” but the deal is already under a reported Department of Justice (DOJ) inquiry. The lawsuit’s outcome has implications for future license-plus-hire deals. Groq told CNBC the suit is “meritless” and said its licensing agreement with Nvidia “delivered exceptional value for Groq, our investors, and our employees.”

The deal involved both the LPU technology and the people who built it , including Ross, a former Google TPU engineer who founded Groq in 2016. The LP30 has 500MB SRAM per die and 150 TB/s bandwidth, uses Samsung’s 4nm process technology , and is rated by Nvidia at up to 1.23 FP8 PFLOPS. A single LPX rack has 256 LPUs with 128GB SRAM, 40 PB/s, and 315 FP8 PFLOPS in aggregate, as a decode co-processor for Vera Rubin NVL72. The LP30 appears to be the next-gen LPU Groq roadmapped in August 2023 on Samsung’s SF4X process with its first-gen Tensor Streaming architecture.

During Hot Chips in August of this year, Igor Arsovski, Groq’s former chief architect and now Nvidia VP of hardware, called the occasion “a pinch me moment for the Groq team that’s now integrated into the Nvidia group.” The rack was already in production at the time, Arsovski said. This supports the complaint’s factual premise, but does not answer the legal question about whether more is owed.

Nvidia’s 10-K notes indicate that “no customer contracts, existing products, or equity interests were purchased” with “$13.0 billion paid at closing and $4 billion, inclusive of imputed interest, payable within one year.” The goodwill number, as reported above, is about 85% of the $16.9 billion Nvidia booked and around 5.8x the value of the technology asset. Nvidia put significantly more value on the LPU design team and the technology’s future development than on the design itself.

Groq said when the deal was announced that it would continue “to operate as an independent company,” and it joined the Nvidia Cloud Partner program in August. Also in August, “Groq LLC” had a $350 million Series A and a $3.5 billion valuation after raising $650 million in June. Before the deal, in September 2025, the valuation was put at $6.9 billion after a $750 million round. Groq says it now operates 13 data centers and expects to scale from 54 to 200+ MW in 2027. Nvidia was slated to participate in the Series A, which Groq says will support those seeking “clusters of NVIDIA accelerated computing.”

Groq also said in August that it is “among the first adopters of NVIDIA Groq 3 LPX” with Nvidia’s Vera Rubin NVL72, deploying with Dell . Those racks are built on the LPU technology Groq licensed to Nvidia, and Groq claims to be “the only team with hands-on experience operating LPUs in production at scale.” The Financial Times said Groq “pivoted entirely to AI cloud computing, dropping its chip design efforts.”

The suit alleges that the Groq board was conflicted, failing to secure the best terms for every shareholder and denying some of them a vote on the deal. Specifically, it says Ross and other top Groq employees were allowed to “take a discount on those shares and be paid separately for following the technology to Nvidia.” According to the suit, Nvidia hired “nearly all” of Groq’s engineers, as many as 200. However, the final payout is alleged to have ignored potential upside and synergies with Nvidia.

The plaintiffs also say that because Nvidia didn’t buy Groq outright, the $17 billion license payment was taxable as income at Groq, and that the Series A valued the remaining Groq above the price paid to the shareholders who were bought out. They say four “conflicted funds” on Groq’s board, BlackRock, Social Capital, Infinitum, and Disruptive, which are not named as defendants in the case, engineered that gap and profited by staying with Groq after the buyout.

As reported by Axios in December 2025, though, sources close to the deal said that most shareholders would get per-share payouts “tied to the $20 billion valuation.” Around 90% of employees would join Nvidia, with vested shares paid in cash and unvested shares paid in vesting Nvidia stock. Staff who stayed with Groq would be paid for vested shares and get a package including “economic participation in the ongoing company.”

As for the DOJ, the New York Times reported in September that the department sent Nvidia a formal request for information with a fine being possible. Nvidia said at the time that the Groq story was “a prime example of the American system working as designed.” The deal did not go unnoticed by some senators who, in February, put it under the “reverse acqui-hire” deal label. Federal Trade Commission Chair Andrew Ferguson said in January that the agency is “beginning to examine these acqui-hires to make sure they are not an attempt to get around” its merger review process.

The litigation comes not long after Nvidia’s agreement to acquire Hugging Face (HF) a month ago, which included a purchase price and equity for HF employees who join Nvidia, a similar split. The deal is waiting on approval, but unlike the Groq deal, it is an outright purchase of the company. When the Groq deal was announced, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang told employees in an email, obtained by CNBC , that while Nvidia was adding Groq staff and licensing its IP, “we are not acquiring Groq as a company.”

The legal question on the Groq deal remains open, and more details will come out as the case proceeds and the defendants respond. As for the LPX customers, Nvidia calls Nebius the first AI cloud to adopt LPX and says the racks will be online there later this year. Looking ahead, Nvidia has the LP35, with NVFP4 support, alongside the Rubin Ultra and LP40 for Feynman on its roadmap .

item.title: Musk rejects rumors of TSMC takeover of Terafab — Intel reaffirms 14A node deal as Musk floats cleanroom 'sublease'
item.description:
Intel will remain a part of Elon Musk's Terafab project, Lip-Bu Tan, chief executive of Intel, told reporters on Wednesday. Around the same time, Elon Musk, chief executive of SpaceX, Tesla, and xAI, said that Terafab remains committed to building and operating its fab itself, but proposed to lease a part of the fab to TSMC.

Intel will continue its involvement in Terafab, Lip-Bu Tan told Bloomberg prior to the company's event in Japan that commemorates the company's presence in Japan. Back in April, Intel and Terafab, the semiconductor production venture by SpaceX, Tesla, and xAI, announced that the new chipmaker would use Intel's next-generation 14A fabrication process to make chips. Details of the collaboration are still unknown, but there is a general understanding that Intel will license its manufacturing technology to Terafab, though it is unclear whether it will also help ramp up production using the node.

At around the same time, Elon Musk debunked rumors that his companies would invest in Terafab and then partner with TSMC, which will build and operate the fab. Instead, Elon Musk proposes that TSMC sublease a part of Terafab to make chips for its customers.

"No, we will build and run the fab," Elon Musk wrote in an X post . "Let there be ZERO doubt about that. Maybe TSMC subleases part of the Terafab if they want, but nothing more than that."

Offering TSMC, the world's largest foundry that owns and operates dozens of advanced 300-mm fabs around the world, to 'sublease' a part of Terafab is quite an unusual arrangement for many reasons.

First up, TSMC has its own production facilities as well as aggressive plans for about 10 new fab phases in the coming years, and it hardly needs to sublease any capacity or part of the building or site from a third party.

Secondly, semiconductor fabs are not generic facilities: if Terafab is initially equipped and qualified around Intel's 14A process technology, converting part of the facility for TSMC's A14, A13, or A12 processes that the company will use in the back half of the decade would require different process flows, equipment configurations, materials, automation, qualification, and contamination control. Theoretically, TSMC could install a largely independent production line within the same enormous building, but at that point the arrangement would resemble TSMC building and operating its own fab inside a Musk-controlled site rather than simply renting spare manufacturing capacity.

Thirdly, if Intel licenses 14A technology to Terafab, the agreement would almost certainly contain extensive provisions governing access to Intel IP, process information, equipment configurations, and personnel. Putting TSMC engineers and manufacturing operations inside the same facility could create contractual and IP-isolation issues even if TSMC never directly touches the Intel production line. In fact, IP protection would be extraordinary at Terafab, which will complicate its operation.

Fourthly, if indeed two chipmakers end up in the same fab building, or even in the same campus, responsibility for downtime becomes messy. In the case of a Terafab-owned power distribution system, water plant, chemical system, or cooling installation fails and takes someone's production offline, determining operational responsibility and financial liability for potentially hundreds of millions of dollars of affected wafers would be considerably more complicated than at a site controlled by one company.

Finally, if Terafab can equip enough cleanroom space by the end of the decade to satisfy semiconductor requirements of Tesla, SpaceX, and xAI while still leaving substantial capacity available to TSMC, that would raise questions about whether the project had significantly overbuilt capacity in its initial phases.

Since Musk's statements at X are deliberately vague, it is hard to interpret them. In fact, there might be a conceptual problem with Musk's statement. If TSMC installs its own tools, hires its own employees, brings process technology, and production management, while Terafab just provides land, shell, and infrastructure, calling this a 'sublease' undersells what would be a TSMC fab embedded within the Terafab campus. Alternatively, if Terafab provides the tools and infrastructure and TSMC just operates them, that starts to look much closer to precisely the kind of TSMC operational involvement Musk appears to be denying.

Anyhow, while Intel has confirmed its involvement in the project and Musk wants TSMC to be part of it as well, the latest comments raise more questions than they answer.

item.title: Seagate and Toshiba battle for TDK's HDD head business, a critical hard drive component — multi-billion-dollar deal threatens sole independent supplier as shortages intensify
item.description:
Seagate Technology and Toshiba are reportedly competing to acquire TDK's hard disk drive magnetic head business in a transaction valued at several billion dollars, reports Bloomberg . For Seagate, the acquisition would expand the supply of HDD heads that it also produces internally, but for Toshiba, TDK is the only way for it to get magnetic heads for its hard drives. If Seagate buys TDK's HDD heads operation, then Toshiba's HDD business will depend on supply from Seagate.

TDK is the world's only independent supplier of HDD magnetic heads and Toshiba's sole source of the components. By contrast, Seagate and Western Digital manufacture heads internally and also buy them from TDK if they need to. In recent years, TDK started to produce HDD heads for Seagate's drives that rely on heat-assisted magnetic recording (HAMR) technology, Western Digital's products featuring energy-assisted magnetic recording (EAMR), and Toshiba's HDDs based on microwave-assisted magnetic recording (MAMR) technology, which makes it an important supplier for all hard drive manufacturers.

Yet, while Seagate and Western Digital produce magnetic heads internally, they also source them from TDK when they need additional supply to respond to increases in demand. Toshiba, by contrast, depends entirely on TDK for these components. Access to TDK's technology is particularly important for Toshiba as while the company's next-generation 30TB-class HDDs are expected to rely on MAS MAMR technology, their successors will rely on HAMR. Meanwhile, developing write and read heads for HAMR is particularly hard and time-consuming, which makes TDK a key enabler for Toshiba's HDD business both for existing products (for which the company probably has long-term supply agreements) and future generations of hard drives that only exist in the roadmap.

Toshiba reportedly approached TDK about acquiring its HDD head operation in spring 2026. Seagate subsequently entered negotiations in summer with a higher offer, according to people familiar with the discussions, Bloomberg said. The potential acquisition could be worth as much as several billion dollars.

Control of TDK's magnetic-head operation could significantly alter the competitive balance of the HDD industry. The successful bidder would control the industry's only independent head supplier, which will potentially give it greater influence over pricing and make it more difficult for competitors to rapidly increase HDD output. Both Toshiba and Seagate are therefore reportedly concerned about maintaining access to TDK heads if the rival bidder acquires the business.

For TDK, a sale would provide an opportunity to exit an historically volatile, relatively low-margin business that requires continuous investment as magnetic recording technologies advance. The company has been directing more resources toward batteries, passive components, and sensors in anticipation of increased AI-related demand from devices such as smart glasses. Selling the HDD-head business could provide additional capital to accelerate investments in these areas.

Executives from Seagate, Toshiba, and TDK reportedly met in Tokyo last week to discuss mechanisms that could preserve supplies of magnetic heads, including a possibility of creating a joint venture. The negotiations remain preliminary and could ultimately produce no transaction. While Seagate and TDK reportedly declined to comment on the Bloomberg report, Toshiba denied that any meeting took place, as well as its plans to acquire HDD heads production capability.

It should be noted that any acquisition would likely face regulatory scrutiny because of the concentrated nature of the HDD market and TDK's unique position in it. TrendForce estimates that Seagate and Western Digital each account for approximately 45% of HDD shipments in terms of bits shipped, whereas Toshiba controls around 10%.
